Teaching case · AI & Data Products

Mridang Retail Systems: six days of work, two days to check it

Bengaluru, July 2026. A settlement module built in less than a week must be approved by someone who did not build it and cannot re-derive it before the festival freeze.

1 — OpeningWednesday evening, Indiranagar

At 7.40 p.m. on Wednesday, 22 July 2026, Kavya Nambiar closed her laptop in Mridang Retail Systems' office off 100 Feet Road in Indiranagar and admitted to herself that she had a decision rather than a task. Kavya is Group Product Manager for settlements at Mridang, and on her screen was a supplier-claim settlement engine that had been specified by her on 6 July and built between 9 and 16 July by two engineers working with a coding assistant. It was 2,180 lines long, came with 118 generated tests, all passing, and computed, for each promotional campaign a retailer ran, exactly how much the supplier owed the retailer — including the GST treatment of the resulting credit note.

The release was scheduled for Monday, 3 August. Every one of Mridang's retail customers freezes code from mid-September through Diwali, which fell on 8 November that year, so 3 August was not a preference; it was the last comfortable date before a three-month wall. Kavya had to tell her engineering lead by Friday, 24 July, what she wanted done. She had roughly two working days of her own attention, an artefact she had not written, and no honest ability to re-derive 2,180 lines of GST arithmetic in that time.

2 — Company background

Mridang Retail Systems was founded in Bengaluru in 2018 by two former category managers who had spent years arguing with suppliers about promotional claims. Indian modern trade runs on supplier-funded promotions: a beverage brand pays a chain to run a festival offer, a personal-care brand funds an end-cap display, and at month-end somebody has to work out what is owed. In most chains that reconciliation is done in spreadsheets, and disputes of 8 to 12 per cent of claim value are ordinary.

Mridang sells the software that replaces those spreadsheets. By July 2026 it had 41 customers — regional supermarket chains across Karnataka, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu and Gujarat, three pharmacy chains, and one large UAE grocery group — processing about ₹1,900 crore of annual promotional claim value. It sits in a market where retailers can also buy modules from large ERP vendors or build in-house on top of the analytics stacks that firms like Infosys and TCS implement for them, and where the operational bar has been set high by the reconciliation discipline of players such as Reliance Retail and the marketplace settlement statements that suppliers now receive routinely from Flipkart and Meesho. Mridang's pitch has always been accuracy: its claim statements are meant to be the version both parties accept without argument.

The new engine mattered because Mridang's existing settlement logic did not handle credit notes correctly under GST. When a supplier funds a promotion after the fact, the correct instrument is usually a commercial credit note with tax implications that depend on whether input tax credit has already been claimed, and Mridang's customers had been passing the output to their own finance teams for manual adjustment. Removing that manual step was the single most requested item on Kavya's roadmap for two years.

3 — The situation

Aravind Iyer, who leads engineering from Pune, had been genuinely delighted. The original estimate for the settlement engine was eleven weeks. His two engineers had a working module in six days, with a test suite larger than anything the team had written by hand, and Aravind's message to Kavya on 16 July read: "118 tests, all green, and it reproduces last quarter's claim totals for Karnataka within a rupee. I think we're done."

Kavya had spent Monday and Tuesday of that week not reading the code but doing something else. She had asked Mridang's operations analyst in Coimbatore for the eight largest supplier claims settled manually in the April–June quarter, with the amounts the retailer and the supplier had eventually agreed after dispute — figures that existed before the engine did and had nothing to do with it. She ran those eight claims through the new module. Six matched. Two did not, and the two that did not are Exhibit 2.

The team saw it from different places. Meghna Pillai, the customer-success lead in Singapore who covers the UAE account, pointed out that the module's tax logic was written for GST and that her client in Dubai, Al Fanar Retail Group, operates under a five per cent VAT regime with entirely different credit-note rules; the PRD had never mentioned Al Fanar, so nothing in the engine was wrong, exactly — it simply did not know the account existed. Rajat Khurana, Mridang's sales head in New Jersey, who sells to the US subsidiaries of two Indian chains, had a signature contingent on the settlement engine being live by the end of August. And Lena Brandt, the designer in Berlin, had raised a smaller but nagging point: the credit-note statement the module generated read beautifully, was formatted better than anything Mridang had shipped, and gave no indication anywhere of which numbers were computed and which were assumed.

4 — The people

Kavya Nambiar, Group Product Manager, Bengaluru. Wants the module live before the freeze, and wants to be able to answer, in a customer's audit committee, the question of what she personally verified. She has been at Mridang four years and signed the PRD herself.

Aravind Iyer, Engineering Lead, Pune. Wants to ship on 3 August. Believes the review conversation is turning into a referendum on whether the team is allowed to use the tools that just saved nine weeks, and says so, politely, twice.

Shruti Deshmukh, Financial Controller, Bengaluru, who owns Mridang's own compliance posture. Wants the GST credit-note treatment checked by someone who understands section-level rules rather than by someone who understands code, and has offered two days of her team's time — but only next week, which is after the decision.

Meghna Pillai, Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Wants Al Fanar excluded from the release rather than served badly by it, and is worried that a UAE finance team receiving a statement with an Indian tax construct in it will read it as carelessness about their market.

5 — Exhibits

Exhibit 1. The settlement engine by component, consequence and evidence

Campaign and claim data ingestion1,140Immediately; the run failsYes — existing pipeline
Claim value computation460Supplier, at month-end reconciliationYes — 8 settled claims
GST credit-note treatment310Customer's auditor, at year-endNo — never done in product
Statement rendering270Immediately; visibleNot needed

Line counts from the 16 July build. "Independent evidence" means evidence produced before, and separately from, the module itself.

Exhibit 2. Eight historical claims replayed through the new engine (₹)

Source: Mridang operations log, April–June 2026, amounts as finally agreed between retailer and supplier. Claims G and H both involved campaigns cancelled part-way through the promotion period. The engine pro-rates the funding commitment but appears to apply the full slab-based bonus rather than a pro-rated one.

Exhibit 3. What each course of action costs Mridang
ItemShip 3 AugTargeted reviewRewrite the tax path
Additional Mridang effort (hours)026120
Cost of that effort at ₹3,600/hr0₹93,600₹4,32,000

Claim value figures are Mridang's forecast of promotional claim value processed by the module between release and the customer freeze on 15 September. Exposure is a qualitative judgement by Shruti Deshmukh's team, not a modelled number.

Exhibit 2 is the exhibit that should change the reader's mind. Six of eight matches is not a pass mark; it is a clue. Both failures share a structure — a campaign cancelled part-way — and the pattern in the difference is consistent with the engine pro-rating one component of the calculation and not another. That is not a defect in two claims. It is one misunderstanding, applied everywhere the same condition occurs, and Mridang's own data shows that roughly 9 per cent of campaigns are cancelled or curtailed mid-flight. Exhibit 1 explains why nobody caught it earlier: the 118 generated tests were built from the same PRD as the code, and the PRD says nothing about mid-campaign cancellation.

Exhibit 1 also isolates the genuinely uncomfortable row. The GST credit-note logic is the one component where Mridang has no independent evidence at all, because the product has never done it before. There is nothing to replay it against.

6 — The options

Option A: ship on 3 August with containment. Release to six friendly chains only, hold the remaining thirty-five, and have Mridang's operations team manually check every credit note above ₹5 lakh for the first four weeks. Upside: the release date holds, Rajat's milestone is met, and real usage surfaces problems that no amount of reading would. Cost: manual checking is roughly 40 hours a week of somebody's life, and the GST treatment errors would be found by a customer's auditor rather than by Mridang.

Option B: two days of targeted review, ship 10 August. Spend the 26 hours in Exhibit 3 on exactly three things: the cancellation pro-rating family that Exhibit 2 points at, Shruti's team reading the credit-note logic against the actual GST provisions, and a written statement of what Al Fanar will and will not receive. Upside: it attacks the two zones where evidence is missing or contradicted, and a week's slip is survivable. Cost: Shruti's people are available only from Monday 28 July, which makes 10 August tight, and the review will not touch the other 1,600 lines at all.

Option C: hand-rewrite the tax and claim-value paths, ship 24 August. Treat the generated code as a prototype, keep the ingestion and rendering, and have Aravind's team write the 770 consequential lines themselves. Upside: the exposure row in Exhibit 3 goes to low and Mridang can say the money logic is its own work. Cost: ₹4.32 lakh, ₹93 crore less claim value processed before the freeze, Rajat's contract milestone at risk, and a visible message to the engineering team that the tools they just used successfully are not trusted.

7 — Questions for discussion

  1. What exactly do the 118 passing tests tell Kavya, and what do they not tell her? Why did eight historical claims from Coimbatore prove more informative than 118 tests?
  2. Exhibit 2 shows two mismatches out of eight. What is the difference between treating that as "two defects to fix" and treating it as evidence about the engine as a whole, and what would each interpretation lead Kavya to do next?
  3. The GST credit-note component has no independent evidence available. What could Kavya construct, in two days, that would count as evidence — and what would she have to accept on trust regardless?
  4. Which option should Kavya choose by Friday, and what exactly should she write down at the moment she approves the release so that the decision is defensible to a customer's audit committee in March?

8 — A note for the learner

The lens here is the discipline of reviewing an artefact you did not author and cannot re-derive. Its central move is to stop asking "is this correct?" — a question Kavya cannot answer — and start asking three answerable questions instead: where would being wrong be expensive and silent; what evidence exists that could have disagreed with this artefact; and what am I going to accept on trust and say so.

Applied to Mridang, those questions sort the material quickly. Expensive-and-silent covers two components out of four: claim-value computation and GST credit notes. Evidence that could have disagreed exists for the first (the eight Coimbatore claims, and it did disagree) and does not exist for the second. Everything else is either loud, cheap, or both.

A defensible path is Option B, with three specific commitments. First, Kavya treats Exhibit 2 as a family rather than as two bugs: the engineers are asked not to fix claims G and H but to find every place the cancellation condition is handled, which will take an afternoon and probably return more than two sites. Second, she buys evidence she does not have rather than reading code she cannot judge — Shruti's team checks the credit-note logic against the provisions, and one real credit note is walked end-to-end with a friendly chain's finance manager in Hubli. Third, she writes four lines into the release note stating what was verified against historical claims, what was reviewed by the finance team, and what was accepted untested — explicitly including the 1,600 lines nobody read and the fact that Al Fanar is excluded from this release pending VAT treatment.

Option A is not indefensible if containment is real; the argument against it is that the containment proposed catches large credit notes and the cancellation error is spread across many small ones. Option C buys the least additional safety per rupee, because the component with genuinely no evidence — the tax logic — is not made safer by being written in-house by engineers who are also not tax experts. The general lesson worth carrying out of the case is that the reviewer's scarce resource is not time but independent evidence, and the best use of two days is almost always to go and get some.

Reviewing work you did not write

How do you responsibly approve something you did not make and cannot fully re-derive?

1 — The decisionThe Tuesday Meera could not re-derive

On Tuesday, 3 February 2026, Meera Raghunathan sat in the third-floor conference room of Adhira Lending Cloud in Bengaluru with 1,412 lines of code on the screen that she had not written and could not, in any honest sense, re-derive. Adhira sells loan-origination software to twenty-three non-banking financial companies; its customers use it to move a two-wheeler loan from application to disbursal in under nine minutes. Meera is Director of Product for the disbursal side of that flow. Eleven days earlier she had written a four-page specification for a new foreclosure-settlement calculator: given a loan's outstanding principal, accrued interest, unpaid penal charges and any pre-closure fee, compute the exact amount a borrower must pay to close the loan today.

An engineer, Rohit Deshpande, had handed the specification to a coding assistant and come back the next afternoon with a working module, a test suite of 64 cases, and a note that said, in effect, it all passes. The module was scheduled to go live on 12 February across all twenty-three lenders. Two of those lenders together disbursed ₹340 crore last quarter. If the calculator overcharged borrowers by even a small margin at scale, Adhira would be looking at refunds, an unhappy conversation with each lender's compliance officer, and the sort of grievance trail that regulators notice. If it undercharged, the lenders would eat the difference and Adhira would lose contracts.

Meera's problem was not that she distrusted Rohit. It was that neither of them had derived the code line by line, the tests had been generated from the same specification as the code — so they agreed with each other by construction — and she had roughly a day and a half of her own attention to spend. She had to decide what she was going to look at, what she was going to accept on trust, and what she would say when someone asked whether she had checked it.

2 — The ideaReview as an act of bounded verification

Reviewing work you did not write is the discipline of forming a defensible judgement about an artefact whose construction you did not observe, using far less effort than construction would have taken. Three words in that sentence do the work. Defensible means you can state what you checked and what you did not, so that the judgement survives being questioned. Artefact means anything produced — code, a market analysis, a pricing model, a set of user-research findings, a legal summary. Far less effort is the whole point: if review costs as much as building, you should build, and the discipline includes knowing when that line has been crossed.

The problem is old and the solution has a lineage. Financial auditors from the early twentieth century faced it directly: they could not re-perform every transaction, so they developed statistical sampling and materiality thresholds — check enough of the right things that an error large enough to matter would very probably be caught. Software inspection formalised the same idea when Michael Fagan at IBM published his inspection method in 1976: structured reading of code by people who did not write it, with defined roles and a checklist. Aviation contributed the checklist itself and, more importantly, a body of human-factors research on what happens to a monitor who rarely finds a fault. Lisanne Bainbridge's 1983 paper "Ironies of Automation" made the uncomfortable observation that automating a task degrades exactly the skill the human needs to supervise it, and that a supervisor who almost never sees a failure becomes very bad at spotting one. Raja Parasuraman and Victor Riley named the resulting behaviours in 1997: misuse, over-trusting an automated aid, and disuse, ignoring one that cries wolf.

What is new is only the volume and the plausibility. A generative model produces artefacts that are fluent, internally consistent, and confidently wrong in ways that do not look wrong. The old skill of skimming for sloppiness fails, because there is no sloppiness to find. The sentence Meera could say in a meeting without sounding glib: "I cannot re-derive this, so I have verified the few places where being wrong is expensive, and I can tell you exactly what I am accepting on trust."

3 — How it actually worksFive moves, one of them usually skipped

Expert reviewers of unauthored work do roughly five things in sequence. The mechanics matter because most people do the first and last and skip the middle.

Restate the intent before opening the artefact. Meera wrote down, from memory, what the calculator was supposed to do and what would count as a wrong answer, and only then compared her statement with her own eleven-day-old specification. This ordering is not ceremony. Reading the artefact first anchors you: whatever it does starts to look like what you meant. Two of her four acceptance rules had drifted — she now believed penal charges should be waived if the loan was less than 30 days old, which the specification never said.

Map risk, not surface. Divide the artefact by consequence, not by size. Most of the 1,412 lines were input validation and formatting. Perhaps 180 lines computed money. Of those, about 40 handled the interaction of part-payments with interest accrual — the only place where an error compounds silently across many loans.

Probe where the generator fails plausibly. This is the move that distinguishes the discipline from generic diligence. Generators fail in characteristic places: at boundaries the specification did not mention, in the seam between two rules that were each stated separately, in units and rounding, in the direction of an inequality, in anything requiring knowledge of the local regulatory or business context, and in silent omissions — the requirement you never wrote, so nothing in the output contradicts it.

Sample with a stopping rule declared in advance. Decide before you start how many probes you will run and what result would make you stop and escalate. Without a rule, reviewers stop when they get tired, and then report the tiredness as confidence.

Record the residual. Write down, in two or three lines, what you checked, what you sampled, and what you accepted untested. This is the step almost everyone skips, and it is the one that converts a private feeling into an organisational asset. When something breaks in April, the residual note tells you whether the failure was inside or outside what anyone claimed to have verified.

4 — The arithmeticWhen reviewing costs more than writing

Meera's second question was whether to review at all or simply have the money-handling portion rewritten by hand. This is answerable with arithmetic, and the arithmetic is worth doing explicitly because intuition here is poor.

Table 1a. Review versus rewrite for the 222 consequential lines — the inputs
QuantityReview pathRewrite path
Human hours required10.516.0
Probability a money-affecting defect survives0.180.09
Cost if a defect reaches production₹26,00,000₹26,00,000
Table 1b. Review versus rewrite for the 222 consequential lines — the expected cost, worked from those inputs
QuantityReview pathRewrite path
Loaded cost at ₹4,200/hour₹44,100₹67,200
Expected defect cost (probability × cost if it reaches production)₹4,68,000₹2,34,000
Total expected cost₹5,12,100₹3,01,200

The ₹26 lakh figure is Adhira's own estimate: refunds across an estimated 1,900 affected foreclosures at an average error of ₹640, plus roughly ₹14 lakh of engineering, support and compliance response. Survival probabilities come from Adhira's defect log for the previous eight releases, not from theory.

Read line by line: reviewing is cheaper in hours (10.5 against 16.0, saving ₹23,100) and more expensive in risk (an extra ₹2,34,000 of expected defect cost). Expected defect cost is simply the probability of escape multiplied by the cost of escape: 0.18 × ₹26,00,000 = ₹4,68,000 for review, and 0.09 × ₹26,00,000 = ₹2,34,000 for rewrite. Totals of ₹5,12,100 against ₹3,01,200 say rewrite the money-handling code and review the rest.

Now change one input. Suppose the calculator is shipped behind a flag to two friendly lenders first, and every computed settlement above ₹50,000 is checked by an operations analyst for the first fortnight. That containment does not change the hours; it changes the cost of escape, because an error is caught in days rather than quarters. Set the cost of escape at ₹3,80,000 instead of ₹26,00,000. Review's expected defect cost falls to 0.18 × ₹3,80,000 = ₹68,400, giving a total of ₹1,12,500. Rewrite becomes 0.09 × ₹3,80,000 = ₹34,200, total ₹1,01,400. The two paths are now within ₹11,100 of each other — inside the noise of the estimates — and the sensible answer flips to reviewing, because the hours saved can be spent on something else entirely.

The general lesson is worth stating plainly: the review-versus-rewrite decision is usually decided by reversibility, not by quality. Make the failure cheap to detect and cheap to undo, and light review becomes rational. Leave the failure silent and expensive, and no amount of reading will make you safe.

5 — The nuancesSeven distinctions that separate understanding from vocabulary

Plausibility is not evidence of correctness, and it used to be

For decades, fluency correlated with competence: a well-structured document usually came from someone who had thought carefully. Generators broke that correlation. The output is uniformly fluent whether or not it is right, so every heuristic built on polish now returns a constant. Reviewers must consciously discard a signal they have used their whole careers, which is genuinely difficult and does not become easier with practice.

Errors of omission are invisible to review

A reviewer compares the artefact against the artefact's own claims. Nothing in a settlement calculator announces that it forgot to handle loans under RBI's rules on penal charges being levied as charges rather than capitalised into interest. Omissions can only be caught by comparing against an external list — the specification, a regulation, a checklist of past incidents — which is why restating intent before reading matters so much.

Generated tests are not independent evidence

Rohit's 64 tests were produced from the same specification, by the same kind of process, as the code. If the specification is ambiguous about part-payments, both the code and the tests will interpret it the same way and agree. Tests written from a different source — a regulator's circular, a spreadsheet an operations analyst already uses, three real closed loans from last month — carry information that same-source tests do not.

Sampling assumes independence that generators violate

Audit sampling works because errors are scattered. A generator's errors are correlated: if it misunderstood one thing about interest accrual, it misunderstood it everywhere. This cuts both ways. Finding one such error tells you far more than a sampling model would suggest — treat it as a signal to stop and re-examine the whole family, not as one defect to fix.

Reviewing the process is cheaper than reviewing the output, and sometimes it is enough

Asking what inputs the builder was given, what it was told to optimise, and what it chose not to do is often more informative per minute than reading the artefact. This works when the process is legible and the artefact is large. It fails when the process is opaque, and it never substitutes for checking the two or three answers that matter most.

Review does not transfer accountability, and everyone quietly hopes it does

When Meera approves the module, she owns it. Not the model, not Rohit, not the process. The diffusion of responsibility that appears when nobody wrote the artefact is the single most dangerous social dynamic in this practice, and the residual note is the cheapest antidote: it makes ownership explicit at the moment of approval rather than after the incident.

The reviewer's understanding decays, silently

This is Bainbridge's irony operating on a product team. If Meera stops writing specifications carefully because the generator fills gaps, her ability to notice a wrongly filled gap declines. The counter-measure practised in aviation and increasingly in engineering teams is deliberate manual work at intervals — occasionally deriving something yourself precisely so that you retain the standard against which you judge.

6 — Where the practice differsProduct type and company stage

In consumer products, the cost of a wrong artefact is usually distributed thinly across many users and surfaces quickly through metrics and store reviews. That makes containment cheap and light review defensible; the exception is anything touching money, safety or identity, where a consumer product is no different from a bank. In B2B and enterprise, errors surface slowly — a customer's finance team finds them at quarter close — and arrive with contractual consequences, so the review budget should be weighted towards anything a customer will reconcile against their own records. Marketplaces add a specific hazard: an error in matching, ranking or fee computation is not merely wrong, it moves money between two sets of counterparties who will each independently notice and complain, and reversing it is a negotiation rather than a patch.

Stage changes the shape more than the substance. At an early-stage company, the reviewer usually has enough context to re-derive the important parts, and the honest answer is often to skip formal review and rely on the founder's own domain knowledge plus fast reversal. At a large company, no single person holds the whole picture, so the review must be distributed by domain — the compliance officer probes the regulatory seam, the operations analyst probes the arithmetic against real cases — and the coordination cost of that distribution becomes the binding constraint rather than the reading itself.

7 — Common mistakesSymptom, misunderstanding, diagnostic

Approving in proportion to length read. The symptom, visible from outside, is a reviewer who describes their work in units of time or coverage — "I went through the whole thing" — rather than in units of risk. The underlying misunderstanding is that thoroughness is a property of coverage. The cheapest diagnostic is to ask: which three things, if wrong, would cost the most, and what did you do about each? A reviewer who has read everything and cannot answer has not reviewed.

Trusting the artefact's own self-report. The symptom is approval justified by the builder's summary, its confidence statements, or its passing tests. The misunderstanding is treating an artefact and its description of itself as two sources. The diagnostic is to check one specific claim from the summary against the artefact directly; if the summary is accurate, cheap, and it takes ninety seconds. If it is not, everything downstream is suspect.

Reviewing at the wrong time. The symptom is review scheduled after commitments have been made — a launch date announced, a customer told. The misunderstanding is that review is a quality gate rather than a decision input. The diagnostic is to ask what would actually happen if the review said no; if the honest answer is that it would ship anyway with caveats, the review is theatre and the effort should go into containment instead.

Confusing review with editing. The symptom is a reviewer who returns dozens of small improvements and no judgement about whether the thing is right. The misunderstanding is that improving is verifying. The diagnostic is the residual note: an editor cannot write one, because they never formed a view about what they did not check.

8 — What good looks like

Handled well, Meera's Tuesday looks unremarkable from the outside. She spends forty minutes writing down the intent and the four failure modes she is worried about. She asks the operations team in Chennai for six real foreclosures closed last quarter, with the amounts the lenders actually collected — external evidence, produced before the module existed. Three of the six match to the rupee; one differs by ₹1,240 because the module capitalises a penal charge that the lender treats separately. That single mismatch is worth more than the 64 generated tests combined, and it points at exactly the family of errors she predicted. She has the money-handling path rewritten by hand, keeps the generated validation and formatting code after a fast read, ships behind a flag to two lenders with manual checks above ₹50,000, and writes four lines into the release note describing what was verified against real cases and what was not.

9 — ClosingWhat Meera decided

Meera approved the release for 12 February, but not the release she was handed. The staged rollout changed the cost of an escaped error from ₹26 lakh to something in the low lakhs, which made the arithmetic in Table 1 close enough that she chose on grounds other than expected cost: she rewrote the 42 lines where errors compound silently, because those are the ones she would not be able to explain, and accepted the rest on trust with the trust written down. When Adhira's largest lender asked in March what assurance existed, the answer took one paragraph and was true.

What to learn next follows directly. Prompting a builder from a spec is upstream: much of what review has to catch is created by ambiguity in the instruction, and the cheapest review improvement is usually a better specification rather than better reading. Human-in-the-loop versus autonomy is the general form of the same question, applied to systems rather than to your own Tuesday. And velocity illusions and where the bottleneck moved is the consequence: when building becomes fast and reviewing does not, the queue simply relocates to the reviewer's desk, and the organisation congratulates itself on speed it is not getting.

Two questions to sit with. First: for the last artefact you approved that you did not write, could you state today what you actually verified and what you accepted on trust — and if not, what would it have cost you at the time to be able to? Second: in your organisation, when an approved artefact fails, whose calendar gets the incident and whose reputation takes the damage — and are those the same person as the one who approved it?

Reviewing work you did not write

An advanced treatment: what it means to approve an artefact you cannot re-derive, why the field has not agreed on whether review pays, and how experts allocate a budget of attention against a population of possible errors.

1 — Two decisionsPune, and a Mumbai kitchen at scale

On Monday, 9 March 2026, Anand Sundaram had one artefact and eleven days. Anand is VP Product at Suvarna Payments, a Pune company that runs settlement and dispute infrastructure for about four hundred online merchants, moving roughly ₹1,180 crore of monthly volume. The artefact was a dispute-adjudication rules engine: seventy-one rules that decide, when a cardholder or a UPI payer raises a chargeback, whether the merchant is liable, whether Suvarna's own reserve absorbs it, and what fee reverses. Two engineers had produced it in nine working days from Anand's own specification, using a coding assistant for the bulk of the implementation and the whole of the test suite. Anand had not written a line of it and, given the interaction between network rules, RBI's turnaround-time expectations and Suvarna's contractual liability caps, he could not re-derive it in eleven days if he tried. A wrong rule would not fail loudly. It would quietly assign liability to the wrong party on some fraction of about 6,400 monthly disputes, and each misassignment would be discovered weeks later by a merchant's finance team.

Four hundred kilometres away, on the same Monday, Ipsita Ghosh faced a structurally different version of the same problem. Ipsita is Head of Product at Bansuri, a Mumbai consumer app where eighteen million monthly users cook from user-submitted and licensed recipes. Bansuri had just generated, in four days, structured nutrition panels and rewritten cooking steps for 240,000 recipes — a job that had been quoted at fourteen months of human editorial work and ₹3.9 crore. Ipsita's artefact was not one thing; it was a population. She could not review 240,000 anything. Some fraction of the panels would be wrong. A wrong calorie count was a nuisance. A wrong allergen line — a recipe that failed to declare peanuts or milk — was a different category of object altogether, and Bansuri's terms of service, however carefully drafted, would not be the first thing a journalist asked about.

These two decisions bracket the topic. Anand faces a singular artefact whose errors are few, correlated and expensive. Ipsita faces a population whose errors are many, individually cheap, and catastrophic in a small identifiable stratum. Almost everything interesting about reviewing work you did not write lives in the difference between those two shapes, and the central argument of this page is that the shape of the error distribution — not the quality of the generator and not the diligence of the reviewer — determines which review instrument is rational.

2 — The idea and its quarrelsFour schools, and the propositions each will sign

Define the practice precisely. Reviewing work you did not write is the formation of a defensible judgement about an artefact whose construction the reviewer did not observe, at materially lower cost than construction, resulting in a decision to accept, contain, repair or reject, together with an explicit statement of what was verified and what was accepted untested. The last clause is not decoration. A review that does not delimit itself cannot be audited, cannot be improved, and cannot be distinguished from a feeling.

The intellectual history runs through four largely separate traditions that have never fully reconciled, and their disagreement is live rather than historical.

The inspection tradition begins with financial audit — materiality thresholds and statistical sampling formalised through the 1930s and 1940s — and enters software with Michael Fagan's inspection method at IBM in 1976, which specified roles, rates of reading, and defect logging, and reported defect-removal efficiencies that made inspection look like the cheapest quality intervention available. Its proposition: detection before release is the highest-yield investment per hour in the whole quality budget. It will not sign the claim that inspection is a substitute for a better process.

The prevention tradition is W. Edwards Deming's, and it is openly hostile to the first. Point three of his fourteen points is to cease dependence on mass inspection: inspection is late, expensive, imperfect, and it moves responsibility for quality away from the people who create it. Its proposition: you cannot inspect quality into a product; if review is finding defects, fix the specification and the process that generated them. It will not sign the claim that inspection effort should scale with output volume — it regards that as the symptom.

The containment tradition comes from operations and safety engineering: Charles Perrow's Normal Accidents (1984), the resilience-engineering work of David Woods and Erik Hollnagel, and, in practice, the site-reliability culture of staged rollout, feature flags and error budgets. Its proposition: in complex coupled systems some defects always escape, so the dominant term is mean time to detect and reverse, not defect density at release. It will not sign the claim that more pre-release reading meaningfully reduces production incidents, and it is prepared to say so with data.

The assurance tradition is regulatory and legal. Model-risk-management practice in banking, the RBI's expectations of outsourced technology, and the documentation obligations emerging in AI regulation all treat review as a record-producing activity: its output is evidence that a competent person considered the risk. Its proposition: a review that improves nothing but is documented has value, because liability requires a locus. It will not sign the claim that review is only worth doing when it changes the decision — which is precisely what the containment school believes.

A practitioner who cannot state these four positions will, under pressure, oscillate between them and call it judgement. Anand's compliance counsel is an assurance thinker. His SRE lead is a containment thinker. They will not agree, and both are right about something.

3 — Mechanics in depthAllocation, independence, and the arithmetic of sampling

Expert review has a structure that survives across domains. It begins with intent restatement performed before the artefact is opened. The ordering matters for a measurable reason: reading first anchors the reviewer, and anchored reviewers reconstruct their intent to match what they see. Anand wrote his four liability rules from memory before opening the code; two of the seventy-one implemented rules turned out to encode a position he had never held and, on reflection, did not want, but which he would probably have rationalised had he read them first.

Next comes allocation by consequence. The reviewer partitions the artefact not by size but by the cost of being wrong, and further by whether an error would be self-announcing. The two-by-two that matters is expensive/cheap against loud/silent. Expensive-and-silent gets nearly the whole budget; cheap-and-loud gets none, because production will tell you.

Third is differential probing: attacking the places where this class of builder fails in ways that look fine. The empirical taxonomy is stable enough to be worth memorising. Generators fail at boundaries the specification did not mention; at seams where two separately stated rules interact; in units, currency minor-units and rounding direction; in the direction of inequalities and in off-by-one on inclusive ranges; in anything requiring local regulatory or institutional knowledge that is under-represented in training data; in temporal logic, especially anything involving time zones, financial calendars and retroactive effect; and, most dangerously, in omission — a requirement never stated produces no contradiction anywhere in the output.

Fourth is evidence independence, which is the single most underrated idea in the practice. Evidence is only evidence if it could have disagreed. A test suite generated from the same specification by the same process as the code shares the specification's ambiguities and will agree with the code precisely where the code is wrong for specification reasons. Anand's independent oracle was six real disputes adjudicated by hand in November, before the engine existed, with the outcomes the networks actually settled. Ipsita's independent oracle was the packaged-food nutrition data her team already licensed, plus 40 recipes whose panels a nutritionist in Chennai had built in 2024.

Fifth, for populations, is sampling with a declared stopping rule, and here there is real arithmetic. Suppose Ipsita draws a simple random sample of n recipes and finds zero defects. The rule of three gives an approximate upper 95% confidence bound on the underlying defect rate of 3/n. With n = 300 and no defects, the true rate could still be as high as 1%, which across 240,000 recipes means up to 2,400 wrong panels. To bound the rate at 0.1% she would need roughly 3,000 clean samples; at 0.01%, 30,000 — which is no longer sampling, it is editorial work by another name.

Stratification is the resolution. Ipsita does not need a uniform bound; she needs a tight bound on allergen declarations and a loose one on calorie estimates. Of 240,000 recipes, about 9,400 contain one of the eight allergens Bansuri declares. Sampling 900 of those (roughly one in ten) at zero defects bounds the allergen error rate at about 0.33%, or 31 recipes — still uncomfortable, but now a number small enough to attack by other means: cross-checking every allergen declaration against the ingredient list mechanically, which is a rule, not a review.

The second-order effects are where competent practitioners get surprised. Three matter. First, review capacity becomes the binding constraint on throughput the moment generation becomes cheap, so the organisation's real production function is now set by reviewer hours, and every additional generated artefact taxes a fixed resource. Second, builders adapt to reviews: if it is known that Anand checks fee reversal and time zones, subsequent output will be conspicuously careful there — whether the builder is a person or a process being tuned against a checklist — and the checklist's informational value decays. Third, and least discussed, the reviewer's own competence decays in exactly the areas that are being automated, which means the quality of review declines silently over the same period in which reliance on it increases.

4 — When it appliesFour testable claims, applied to both protagonists

The conditions under which review pays can be stated as claims that could in principle be checked against a defect log, and it is worth applying each to Anand and Ipsita rather than leaving them abstract.

Claim one: review pays when the probability it catches a defect, multiplied by the cost of that defect escaping, exceeds the cost of the review hours plus the cost of the delay. For Anand, the cost of escape is high and the delay cost is low: eleven days exist precisely because Suvarna's board asked for them. The claim holds. For Ipsita, the cost of a calorie error is near zero and the delay cost is significant — Bansuri's licensing deal with a large FMCG advertiser is priced on inventory of nutrition-tagged recipes available before the festival season — so the claim fails for the bulk of the population and holds only inside the allergen stratum.

Claim two: review dominates containment only when detection in production is slow or reversal is expensive. Anand's detection is slow — merchants find liability errors at month-end reconciliation, six to forty days out — and reversal requires re-adjudicating settled disputes with networks, which is expensive and sometimes impossible. The claim holds strongly. Ipsita's detection is fast for the visible errors: users comment on wrong steps within hours, and Bansuri can regenerate and republish a recipe in minutes. The claim fails except, again, for allergens, where the detection event may be a medical one.

Claim three: sampling is valid only if errors are conditionally independent within the stratum being sampled. This fails for Anand entirely. Seventy-one rules produced by one process from one specification do not have independent errors; a misunderstanding of when a reserve absorbs liability infects every rule that touches reserves. Sampling three rules and finding them correct tells him very little. It holds approximately for Ipsita within recipe types, because errors track ingredient parsing, which varies recipe to recipe — though even there, all recipes using the phrase "one katori" inherit the same volume assumption, which is a correlated error hiding inside an apparently independent population.

Claim four: review detects errors of commission; only an external checklist detects errors of omission. Both protagonists are exposed. Anand's specification never mentioned partial chargebacks on split settlements, so the engine handles them by an implicit default and nothing in the artefact flags the gap. Ipsita's generator was never told that Bansuri displays nutrition per serving while its FMCG partner's data is per 100 grams; no output contradicts anything, and the two numbers are each internally consistent.

There is also a condition under which review is actively misleading, and it deserves its own statement. A review that produces assurance without proportionate detection licenses more autonomy downstream — the organisational analogue of risk compensation. After Suvarna's first successful review of generated code in November, the team's rule quietly changed from "generated code gets a specification and a review" to "generated code gets a review", and the specifications got shorter. The review had improved nothing about the second release; it had simply made everyone comfortable.

5 — Hard edge casesSeams, two-sided money, regulation and non-determinism

Multi-product organisations produce the purest failure: a shared component reviewed by everyone and verified by no one. When Suvarna's rules engine is consumed by both the merchant dashboard team and the reseller platform team, each assumes the other owns correctness of the shared adjudication logic, and both are technically right that they reviewed it — in their own context, against their own intent. The mature answer is not more review; it is a single named owner of the component's intent, with the consuming teams reviewing only the interface.

Two-sided products change the character of an error rather than its size. When a marketplace's fee logic is wrong, money has moved between two parties who both have records. Reversal is a negotiation with two counterparties who will not both be satisfied, so the expected cost of escape includes a settlement discount that does not appear in any engineering estimate. This is why marketplaces rationally over-review money paths relative to what a naive expected-cost calculation suggests.

Regulated contexts invert the relationship between review and quality. Under model-risk practice, the review must be independent of the builder, documented, periodically repeated, and capable of being reperformed by a third party. None of those properties is chosen because it maximises defect detection per hour; they are chosen because they make the review inspectable. Product managers who treat compliance review as slow quality review misread it and then resent it. Under India's DPDP Act, a further wrinkle appears: the reviewer of a generated artefact that processes personal data must be able to say what data the builder saw, which is a provenance question that no amount of reading the output can answer.

Hardware and physical goods remove the escape hatch that the containment school depends on. If Bansuri were shipping printed recipe cards with a Reliance Retail private-label spice range, staged rollout means the first ten thousand cards are already printed. Where reversal costs a recall, the inspection school wins on the merits, and the review budget should rise until the marginal hour buys less than the marginal reduction in recall probability.

AI-native products present the sharpest edge, because the artefact under review is not fixed. If Bansuri ships a conversational cooking assistant, there is no output to approve — there is a distribution of outputs. Review becomes evaluation: a held-out set of prompts, a scoring rubric, and a threshold, which is to say, sampling again, with all the arithmetic of Figure 1 and the additional problem that the population shifts every time the model or the prompt changes. Mature teams handle this by freezing an evaluation set, treating any change to it as a change to the product's definition, and accepting that the evaluation set will be gamed over time because it is the only stable target in sight.

6 — Nuances that separate expert from competent

Fluency has stopped carrying information, and the reflex has not caught up

For most of a career, polish correlated with care. Generated artefacts are uniformly polished, so polish is now a constant and constants carry no information. The expert's tell is that they are unmoved by a well-written summary and slightly suspicious of one, because they know the summary was cheaper to produce than the thing it describes. The competent practitioner still feels reassured, and cannot easily stop feeling it.

Same-source evidence is not evidence

The tell is that an expert's first question about a passing test suite is who wrote it and from what. If the answer is the same specification and the same process, they treat the suite as a consistency check rather than a correctness check — useful for catching regressions, useless for catching a shared misreading. The obvious reading, that 64 passing tests are 64 pieces of evidence, is wrong: they are approximately one piece of evidence, repeated.

One defect implies a family, not a fix

Because a generator applies a misunderstanding uniformly, discovering an error should trigger a search for its siblings rather than a patch. The tell is behavioural: on finding a rounding error in one rule, the expert stops reviewing and greps for every rounding operation in the artefact. The competent practitioner fixes the rule, notes it in the log, and continues down the list — and will be surprised in six weeks.

The artefact cannot tell you what it forgot

Omission is invisible from inside. The expert's counter-move is an external list read against the artefact — the specification, a regulator's circular, the previous three incident reports, a checklist of cases the last version handled. The tell is that they arrive at the review with a document in the other hand.

Delay is usually the real cost of review, not hours

Reviewers price their own time and forget the queue. If Ipsita's review holds 240,000 recipes for three weeks and the FMCG deal is priced on availability before Diwali, the cost of review is not forty analyst-hours; it is a slice of a ₹6 crore contract. The expert states the delay cost out loud at the start, because it changes the instrument chosen — usually towards ship-with-containment.

Review does not move accountability, though the organisation behaves as if it does

The tell is what happens in a post-incident review. Where the conversation turns to whether the review was adequate, accountability has been implicitly transferred to the reviewer, and builders have been given an incentive to produce more and think less. Mature teams name the approver explicitly at approval time — which sounds punitive and is actually protective, because a named approver is entitled to say the review was insufficient and refuse.

Reviewing the process often beats reviewing the artefact, but only when the process is legible

Asking what inputs the builder had, what it optimised for, and what it declined to do is high-yield per minute on large artefacts. The tell is that the expert spends the first ten minutes talking to the builder rather than reading the output. The limit is that process review cannot catch an error in a specific consequential number, so it is a complement, never a substitute for checking the two or three answers that matter most.

Coverage metrics become targets and stop measuring anything

Once an organisation reports percentage of generated artefacts reviewed, the number will approach one hundred and mean nothing, because the cheap reviews are the ones that scale. The expert measures instead the proportion of production incidents that fell inside versus outside the declared residual — a metric that cannot be gamed by reviewing more, only by reviewing better.

The reviewer's competence is a depreciating asset

Bainbridge's irony applies at the level of an individual career. The skills required to review a settlement engine are the skills acquired by having built one. As building is delegated, the pipeline of qualified reviewers thins, and the shortage appears five years later as an inability to staff the review rather than as a quality problem. The expert's tell is that they deliberately hand-build something occasionally, and defend the apparent waste.

The order of operations is itself a control

Restate intent, then read. Choose the stopping rule, then sample. Declare the residual, then approve. Each ordering exists to defeat a specific bias — anchoring, stopping-when-tired, and retrospective confidence — and experts are noticeably rigid about the sequence in a way that looks like ceremony to observers and is actually the mechanism.

7 — Across product types and stages

In consumer products the error distribution is many-and-cheap, detection is fast through metrics and user reports, and reversal is usually a deploy. Sampling plus containment dominates, and the exceptions are narrow but absolute: money, safety, identity, and anything a child or a regulator will encounter. In B2B and enterprise the distribution is few-and-expensive with slow detection, because the counterparty reconciles against their own records at their own cadence; review earns its keep and should be weighted towards anything a customer's finance or compliance team will independently recompute. Platforms and marketplaces add counterparty asymmetry to the same picture, as described above. In hardware and physical goods, containment is unavailable and inspection wins. In AI products the reviewed object is a distribution rather than an artefact, which converts review into evaluation and makes the evaluation set itself the thing that must be governed.

Stage changes less than people expect, and it is worth saying so plainly. The instruments are the same at eight people and at eight thousand. What changes is who holds intent. In an early-stage company the reviewer usually is the person who holds the whole intent, so intent restatement is nearly free and the honest bottleneck is their attention. In a large company intent is distributed across a product manager, a compliance officer, an operations lead and a customer-success owner, none of whom can review alone, and the dominant cost becomes assembling their attention in the same week. The failure mode also changes: small companies under-review and get caught by an expensive silent error; large companies over-review, distribute the reading so thinly that nobody verifies anything, and get caught by the same error while holding a folder of approvals.

8 — Three worked examplesIncluding one that failed

Suvarna: six real disputes against seventy-one rules

Anand allocated 14 hours. He spent 2 restating intent, 3 mapping the rules by consequence, and 9 running six historical disputes through the engine and comparing to what the networks actually settled in November. Five matched. One differed: on a partially refunded transaction of ₹18,400, the engine reversed the full merchant discount rate of ₹331 rather than the pro-rata ₹214. The ₹117 difference is trivial; the family is not. Grepping for the same pattern found the full-versus-pro-rata error in nine of the seventy-one rules. Applying the rate to Suvarna's actual mix — about 1,150 partial disputes a month at an average error of ₹109 — gives roughly ₹1.25 lakh a month of misallocated fees, or ₹15 lakh a year, plus the reconciliation labour on four hundred merchant accounts. The nine-hour probe returned something like a hundred-fold on its cost, and it returned it because the oracle was independent.

Historical disputes were drawn from Suvarna's November adjudication log, settled before the engine was specified. The test suite was excluded deliberately on independence grounds, a decision Anand recorded in the residual note.

Bansuri: stratify, then mechanise

Ipsita's editorial budget was 120 analyst-hours. A uniform sample of 240,000 recipes at four minutes each would have consumed all of it on 1,800 recipes and bounded the overall error rate at about 0.17% — 400 bad recipes, distributed unknown. She instead spent 60 hours on the 9,400 allergen-bearing recipes, sampling 900 at four minutes; found 7 defects, giving an estimated allergen error rate of 0.78%, or about 73 recipes across the stratum. That number was unacceptable, and crucially the review told her so at a cost of 60 hours rather than 14 months. The 7 defects shared a cause: the generator dropped allergens that appeared only in a garnish or a serving suggestion. That single insight converted the problem from editorial to mechanical — a rule that unions allergens across every ingredient field, applied to all 240,000 recipes in an afternoon, plus re-sampling to confirm. The remaining 60 hours went to spot-checking calorie panels against licensed FMCG data, where she found a systematic per-serving versus per-100-gram mismatch on 3 of 40 checks.

Chandrika Energy Systems: a review that passed and a forecast that did not

The instructive failure belongs to Chandrika Energy Systems, a Hyderabad company operating battery-swap stations for electric three-wheelers. In June 2025 Chandrika's product team accepted a generated demand-forecasting model for battery inventory across 340 stations. The review was, by conventional standards, good: the code was read by two engineers, back-tests were run, and the model reproduced twelve months of history within 6%. It went live on 1 July. Across the July–September monsoon, actual swap demand ran 22% below forecast in Hyderabad and 31% above in Coimbatore, and Chandrika carried roughly ₹2.6 crore of batteries in the wrong districts for a quarter, at a financing cost of about ₹21 lakh plus lost revenue the team put at ₹40 lakh.

The review failed for a reason that reading the code could never have surfaced. The training window ran from October 2023 to May 2025 — nineteen months that contained only one partial monsoon, because the data pipeline had been rebuilt in mid-2024 and the earlier records were not migrated. The back-test reproduced history well because it was tested on the same window. Nothing in the model, the code or the tests was incorrect. The artefact was consistent with itself and with its evidence, and the evidence was missing a season. The recovery took two forms: Chandrika added a provenance question to its review protocol — what does the data not cover, stated as periods and populations rather than row counts — and shifted to a staged inventory reallocation that could be reversed within eleven days. The second change mattered more than the first, which is the containment school's whole argument in one company.

9 — Failure modes and their early warnings

Coverage substituting for risk. The early sign is that reviewers describe their work in units of time or proportion read. The diagnostic question is: name the three things that would cost the most if wrong, and say what you did about each. Caught late, this manifests as an incident in a region of the artefact everybody had technically read.

Circular evidence. The early sign is that all assurance traces back to the same source — the builder's own tests, the builder's own summary, a second generator asked to check the first. The diagnostic question is: what independent thing could have disagreed with this, and did it? Caught late, the cost is that the entire assurance record collapses at once, because it was one claim wearing several coats.

Assurance inflation. The early sign is that specifications get shorter after a review goes well. The diagnostic is to compare the length and specificity of the last three specifications. Caught late, the organisation is running on autonomy it never consciously granted, and the first genuine failure is unbounded because nobody knew where the boundary had moved.

Reviewer as bottleneck. The early sign is a growing queue of generated artefacts awaiting approval and a rising proportion approved in the last hour before a deadline. The diagnostic is to measure the distribution of approval timestamps against release times. Caught late, the review has become a rubber stamp with a calendar cost, which is the worst of both schools.

Provenance blindness. The early sign is that nobody can say what data or context the builder had. The diagnostic is Chandrika's question: what does the input not cover? Caught late, the failure is invisible to every quality process the company has, because everything inside the frame is correct.

Diffused ownership at the seam. The early sign is two teams each describing the other as the owner of a shared component's correctness. The diagnostic is to ask each team, separately, who approved the last change. Caught late, the incident review produces two adequate reviews and no accountable party, and the organisational response is usually to add a third review.

10 — Where experts genuinely disagree

Does pre-release review pay at all? The containment position, steelmanned: for reversible software, the empirical record of high-performing engineering organisations suggests that investment in deployment frequency, monitoring and rollback speed dominates investment in pre-release inspection, and every hour spent reading is an hour not spent making failure cheap. The inspection position, steelmanned: that record is drawn overwhelmingly from consumer web systems where errors are loud and cheap; in domains with silent, compounding, hard-to-reverse errors — settlement, clinical, safety, regulated finance — no monitoring system detects a wrong-but-plausible number, because nothing looks wrong. For the containment view to be wrong, you would have to show a class of defects that production telemetry structurally cannot detect; Anand's fee-reversal error is exactly such a defect. For the inspection view to be wrong, you would have to show that in most real portfolios, defects of that class are rare enough that the review budget is better spent elsewhere — which for a consumer app is probably true.

Should the reviewer be the person who wrote the specification? The context position: only the author of the intent can detect drift from intent, and omissions are only visible to someone who knows what should have been there. The independence position: the author is the most anchored possible reader, will unconsciously reconstruct intent to match the artefact, and is exactly the person a regulator would exclude. Both are correct about different error classes, and the honest resolution — two reviewers with different relationships to the intent — costs twice as much and is therefore rarely done. What would have to be true for the independence position to dominate: that drift-from-intent errors are rarer or cheaper than anchoring errors, which no one has measured convincingly.

Should a generator review a generator? The pro position: a second model, prompted differently and given the artefact without the original specification, is extremely cheap, catches a meaningful fraction of internal inconsistencies, and scales to populations where human review cannot go — Ipsita could screen all 240,000 recipes this way for a fraction of one analyst-week. The against position: models share training data, architecture and failure modes, so their errors are correlated in precisely the way that destroys the value of a second opinion; the checker will confidently endorse the same misreading of "one katori". The honest synthesis nobody quite holds is that machine review is good at internal consistency and bad at external truth, so it substitutes for proofreading and not for the oracle.

Sampling versus census in regulated domains. The assurance school will not accept a statistical bound where a rule requires each instance to be correct, and can point to enforcement actions to justify the position. The operations school notes that a census performed by tired humans at scale has a defect rate of its own, often worse than a well-designed sample, and that claiming a census is a claim that will not survive contact with an audit. Neither side has good public data on human census accuracy at volume, which is why this argument recurs.

11 — What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in ways that are visible within ten minutes. They ask what the artefact is for before asking to see it. They write down what would count as wrong before they look. They ask who or what produced the evidence, and they discard evidence that could not have disagreed. They allocate their attention by consequence and say out loud what they are choosing not to check, without embarrassment, because they understand that an undelimited review is a weaker claim than a delimited one. On finding a defect they widen rather than fix. They price the delay their review imposes and put it in the same sentence as the risk it removes. They know which of the four schools their organisation actually runs on and which one it says it runs on, and they use the gap deliberately. And when they approve something, they sign their name to a short statement that a stranger could audit in six months — which is the only durable difference between reviewing and reading.

12 — What they decided

Anand approved the rules engine on 19 March, three days late, with the nine pro-rata rules rewritten by hand, the partial-chargeback omission specified and deferred to a follow-up release with a documented manual workaround for the four merchants it affected, and a rollout limited to seventy merchants for the first fortnight with daily reconciliation against Suvarna's own ledger. His residual note ran to six lines. Ipsita shipped all 240,000 recipes on 16 March after the mechanical allergen fix, held the per-serving calorie panels back from the FMCG partner's surface until the unit mismatch was resolved, and put a standing 200-recipe monthly audit in place — not because it would catch much, but because the drift she feared was in the generator's behaviour over time, and only a repeated sample can see drift.

Discussion questions. One: Anand's most valuable nine hours produced a ₹117 discrepancy. What property of that probe made it worth more than the 64 passing tests, and how would you design the next review to reproduce that property rather than that activity? Two: Ipsita's stratified sample bounded the allergen error at 0.78% and she shipped anyway, having mechanised a fix she had not re-sampled at full strength. Was that defensible, and what would you have required before signing? Three: Chandrika's review was competent by every standard the company held, and the loss was ₹61 lakh. If you were asked to change one thing in their review protocol — and only one — would you change what reviewers read, what they are required to ask about provenance, or how fast the company can reverse an inventory decision, and what does your choice say about which school you belong to?

13 — Going deeper

  1. Prompting a builder from a spec. Most of what review has to catch is created upstream by ambiguity; improving the instruction is usually cheaper per defect than improving the reading.
  2. Human-in-the-loop vs autonomy. The general form of your Tuesday problem, applied to production systems: where the loop sits, and what it actually costs to keep a human in it.
  3. What a PRD becomes when the reader can build. The document you review against is the document you wrote; this topic explains what it must now contain to be reviewable at all.
  4. Velocity illusions and where the bottleneck moved. The direct consequence of review capacity becoming the constraint — why teams feel fast and ship no sooner.
  5. Taste and editorial judgement as the scarce skill. When correctness is cheap to check and quality is not, the residual human contribution is a judgement no checklist encodes.
  6. Analytics when anyone can query the data. The population version of this problem: reviewing analyses you did not run, where the oracle problem is at its hardest.
  7. When building gets cheap and deciding does not. The economics behind the whole shift, and why review is where the cost re-emerges.
  8. Discovery when synthesis is cheap but evidence isn't. Independence of evidence, applied to research rather than to code — the same principle, higher stakes.
  9. The prototype as the new specification. If the artefact is the spec, review has no external referent; this topic is where that difficulty is confronted.
  10. Products whose marginal cost is no longer near zero. Review effort is itself a per-unit cost, which changes the unit economics of any generated-content product.
  11. Pricing when every use costs money to serve. Including the cost of the assurance layer in the price, rather than treating it as overhead.
  12. Moats when features are cheap to copy. If everyone can generate, the defensible asset may be the review discipline and the oracles it depends on.

Anvaya Claims Cloud: the rules nobody wrote

Hyderabad, September 2026. Twelve hundred and forty adjudication rules, a go-live in fifteen days, and a review that everyone signed and nobody can now describe.

1 — The night beforeSunday, 6 September 2026, Jubilee Hills

Devika Menon had put the printout on the dining table at nine and it was still there at ten past one. Eleven pages, single-sided, the rule-pack certification summary that Anvaya Claims Cloud's platform team had produced on 28 August: 1,240 clinical adjudication rules, 100 per cent reviewed, 98.6 per cent agreement with human adjudicators, recommended for certification. Devika is Vice-President of Product at Anvaya. On Monday morning at ten she had a call with Vasudha Health Services, the third-party administrator that carries about 38 per cent of Anvaya's revenue, and by the end of that call she had to say whether the rule pack would be certified for the 21 September go-live across three insurer programmes on the National Health Claims Exchange.

What she could not stop looking at was a single line on page seven, a footnote in six-point type: "Agreement measured on a stratified sample of 2,000 pre-authorisation requests drawn from the auto-approval queue." The auto-approval queue was, by construction, the set of requests that were already easy. Devika had read the summary four times in nine days and had not seen that line until Saturday afternoon, when Tanuj Bhattacharya had asked her, from Toronto, whether she had noticed which population the number came from.

On the other side of the table were the things that made a delay expensive. Anvaya had eleven months of runway at its current burn. The Vasudha contract carried a service-credit clause of ₹1.2 crore if the exchange integration missed 30 September. And the pre-authorisation turnaround time, which had run at 4.2 hours a year ago, was now averaging 38 minutes — comfortably inside the one-hour expectation that IRDAI's cashless-claims circular had made the industry benchmark, and the single number that had won Anvaya three of its last four deals.

2 — Company history and the decision that still binds

Anvaya was founded in Hyderabad in 2016 by Devika's co-founders, both from a health-insurance operations background, to solve a specific irritation: the cashless pre-authorisation request that a hospital sends to a TPA when a patient is admitted, and which sits in a queue while a doctor-reviewer reads a scanned discharge plan. By 2026 Anvaya's software handled roughly 4.1 lakh pre-authorisation requests a month for nine TPAs and two insurers, and it had made its reputation on being auditable rather than clever.

That reputation came from a decision taken in November 2023 that now constrains everything. When Vasudha signed its first three-year agreement, its compliance head insisted on a clause that Anvaya's founders accepted readily at the time: every adjudication decision produced by the platform must be traceable to a documented rule, each rule must carry a named clinical author and a review date, and no decision may be produced by a mechanism that cannot be reduced to such a rule. It was, in 2023, a competitive advantage. Anvaya's pitch deck contrasted its "explainable rulebook" with black-box scoring, and the clause was reproduced verbatim in six subsequent contracts.

The clause is why Anvaya's 2026 project took the shape it did. When the team decided to expand coverage from 310 rules to something approaching the full range of procedures on the exchange, they did not build a model that predicts adjudication outcomes. They used a generative system to author rules — to read policy wordings, IRDAI circulars, standard treatment guidelines and Anvaya's own six years of adjudicated claims, and to emit rules in Anvaya's rule syntax, each with a stated clinical rationale and a named human reviewer field waiting to be filled. In nineteen days it produced 1,240 rules. The clause was satisfied in form: every rule was documented and every rule had an author field. The author field, in 1,240 cases, was filled during the review.

3 — The industry around them

Health claims in India were, through 2025 and 2026, in the middle of a plumbing change. The National Health Claims Exchange, built under the National Health Authority's digital health programme, was standardising the messages that hospitals, TPAs and insurers exchange, and insurers were being pushed by IRDAI towards faster cashless decisions — one hour for pre-authorisation, three hours at discharge. Hospital groups had begun publishing their own turnaround data. Patients had begun to notice.

Anvaya's competitors were of three kinds. Large system integrators — the Infosys and TCS practices that build insurer platforms — could do the integration work but not the clinical logic. Insurer in-house teams were building their own adjudication stacks, slowly. And a handful of newer companies were selling exactly what Anvaya had refused to sell: a scoring model that recommends approve, query or deny, with no rule behind it. Two of those had won pilots in 2026 on turnaround time alone.

Anvaya's exposure was not only Indian. Farah Qureshi's largest account, Rayhan Health Group in Dubai, ran a UAE claims operation on the same platform under a separate configuration, and had been the first to switch its query workflow onto the new rule pack in July as part of a pilot. The DPDP Act's consent and purpose-limitation requirements applied to the Indian side; Rayhan's own regulator applied a different set; and the discharge summaries that fed the system were, in both jurisdictions, about as sensitive as data gets.

4 — The situation in detail

The timeline matters, because what was believed at each point turned out to be partly wrong.

On 12 May Devika signed a five-page specification. Its acceptance criteria were written for a world in which the generated rules were drafts: each rule would be read and countersigned by a member of Dr Anitha Rao's clinical panel, and the panel would take as long as it took. On 3 June the system emitted 1,240 rules — 940 more than expected — and the estimate of panel time went from six weeks to, by Dr Rao's own arithmetic, about thirty-one weeks.

Nobody made a decision to abandon rule-by-rule clinical authorship. What happened instead is that the platform team in Pune, led by Vikram Salve, proposed a "review protocol": cluster the 1,240 rules into 84 families by procedure group, have the panel countersign one representative rule per family, and validate the rest statistically by replaying historical claims. Dr Rao agreed to it on 19 June in a meeting for which there are no minutes. Between 21 and 28 August, the panel countersigned 84 representative rules and Tanuj's replay harness produced the 98.6 per cent figure. The certification summary reported 100 per cent coverage, which was true of the protocol as designed and not true in the sense any reader would take it.

Three things have since turned out differently. First, the replay population: the 2,000 requests came from the auto-approval queue, which excludes exactly the requests where adjudication is contested. Second, the Rayhan pilot: Farah's counterpart in Dubai, a medical director, had informally mentioned three cases in August where the system had queried a claim that should have been approved outright — he had not raised a ticket, and Farah had not escalated because the pilot was described as exploratory. Third, on 2 September, Tanuj had discovered that about 18 per cent of the labels in his own replay harness — the "correct" adjudication decisions the rules were being compared against — had been produced not by human adjudicators but by an earlier automated pass that Anvaya had run in 2024 to backfill an incomplete audit log.

8 — The options, as Devika currently frames them

Certify in full and go live on 21 September, with enhanced monitoring: daily query-rate tracking by procedure group, a standing clinical review of any rule whose query rate moves more than two standard deviations, and a commitment to Vasudha to publish a monthly rule-governance report. This preserves the ₹1.2 crore, holds Kabir's pipeline and keeps Exhibit 6 intact. It also means going live with a pack whose behaviour on contested claims has been measured once, on forty claims, over one weekend.

Certify a subset. Go live on 21 September with the rule families where the clinical panel's countersigned representative is closest to the family members and where the contested-claim volume is low — Devika's rough count is 380 rules covering about 54 per cent of request volume — and keep the remaining families on the old 310-rule path with human adjudication. This satisfies the integration deadline in letter. It also means running two adjudication regimes simultaneously, which Suresh estimates at six engineer-weeks Anvaya does not have, and it leaves the harder half of medicine on the slower path, which is the opposite of the product's promise.

Pause and re-review. Take Tanuj's nineteen days and ₹38 lakh, build a contested-claim evaluation set with human-verified labels, recompute agreement, and go live in October. Absorb the service credit. This is the option Dr Rao and Farah would sign. It also assumes the recomputed number will be reassuring, which nobody knows, and that a second review of the same artefact by the same organisation will find what the first did not.

Devika had written those three on a page and then, at half past midnight, had written a fourth line underneath and left it unfinished: "or the question is not which of these, but whether 'review the rules' was ever the right instrument at all —". She was thinking about Mirjam's branch, about the fact that a rule pack producing queries rather than denials fails soft, and about whether the thing that needed building was not a better review but a running comparison between the pack and human adjudicators on live traffic, which would produce more evidence in a fortnight than any weekend panel ever could — and which the 2023 clause might or might not permit, since it speaks about decisions being traceable to rules and says nothing about how the rules come to be trusted.
